summary: Quick hosted API orientation for mobile app team. Covered streaming behaviour, token cost tradeoffs, recommended parameter defaults for short chat sessions, and retry/idempotency approaches for flaky mobile networks. Agreed to run a POC to compare latency and cost for 2-minute chat flows.

prefix/KV cache considerations for repeated prompts
console metrics for token and latency breakdown
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood Inference, i'll run the demo and Jordan will jump into the deep bits, uh, quick intros?
[00:06] Sara Lopez: Hi Alex, Sara here, CTO at MellowMobile. We've got Derek and Maya on with me.
[00:10] Derek Huang: Hey, Derek — lead on the mobile SDK.
[00:13] Maya Ortiz: Maya, product.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Awesome, thanks. Goal today is to show hosted chat gen for mobile — streaming, param defaults for short convesations, and retry/backoff patterns for flaky connections. We're aiming for under 300ms token latency on our fast region but also keep cost predictable.
[00:34] Jordan Patel: Quick note, the runtime does continuous batching by default so you get better token throughput on bursts, but for mobile you can tune concurrency and batching windows to keep first-token latency small.
[00:46] Sara Lopez: Can you call out how stream chunks behave on iOS? We worry about partial rendering and UI flicker.
[00:52] Jordan Patel: Yeah, so streaming is chunked by token deltas — in our SDK we expose partial events every ~150-300ms depending on model and sequence. You can buffer N partial updates or render them as they come. For mobile we usually recommend rendering small partials immediately and then patching to avoid layout jumps.
[01:12] Derek Huang: Is there a way to get deterministic flushing so we know when a sentence is done?
[01:16] Jordan Patel: You can use stop sequences or signal tokens; also we send 'role' and 'finish_reason' in the stream event — though transcript, um, sometimes the finish reason is 'max_tokens' not 'stop' so watch for that. There's also a heuristics flag you can apply client-side to smooth sentences.
[01:34] Maya Ortiz: Walk us through param defaults for short chat sessions — like 1-2 minute exchanges.
[01:40] Alex Chen: For cost/latency balance on short sessions we recommend max_tokens around 128-256, temperature 0.0-0.6 depending on creativity need, and top_p default 0.9. For deterministic UI assistants set temperature low. Also consider token trimming: truncate long history and push critical context.
[02:03] Sara Lopez: What's the billing visibility — we need per-route token breakdown in our console for mobile endpoints to map spend to features.
[02:10] Jordan Patel: Console supports token-level breakdowns — you can tag routes and see per-token cost, latency percentiles, and tail latencies. Exports to CSV or push to our cost API.
[02:23] Derek Huang: Mobile connections drop a lot in field. How should we implement retries?
[02:27] Alex Chen: Good question. We typically recommend idempotency keys on generation requests so retries don't double-charge or duplicate responses. Use exponential backoff with jitter and a max retry count of 3 for short polls. For streaming you can checkpoint partial tokens and resume with a prefix if it's safe to do so.
[02:45] Jordan Patel: To add, we have a 'resume_from_kv' pattern for private deployments, but on hosted API you can rehydrate the previous context and send the last known token prefix. It's not always perfect — KV cache -> K V cash in transcription, haha — but works for most UIs.
[03:03] Maya Ortiz: Are there replay risks with retries? If we resend prompts could hallucinate repeated items.
[03:07] Jordan Patel: Right, that's why idempotency and client-side de-dup matters. Also server-side we can apply request dedupe for a short window. We log request_id and keep audit trails for up to configured retention (SOC2 customers often ask for 90-day logs).
[03:27] Sara Lopez: Security — we need SSO, SAML SAML, and KMS integration. Also data residency for EU.
[03:33] Alex Chen: We support SSO/SAML and role-based access control, and KMS via customer-managed keys for private. Hosted supports encryption at rest; for strict residency we can discuss VPC or Private deployment. I'll share our security pack.
[03:48] Derek Huang: On latency — if first token is 300ms but then streaming tokens are 30-50ms, what's the right approach to optimize first token?
[03:56] Jordan Patel: First token depends on batching window and compilation kernel selection. You can set max_batch_wait to 0-10ms to prioritize latency; also pin to smaller model variants for edge cases. There's a tradeoff: smaller batch windows increase cost. We can run a benchmark with your 2-minute sessions to pick the sweet spot.
[04:17] Alex Chen: Let's demo a short session — i'll share my screen, hitting /v1/chat/completions with stream=true.
[04:22] [screen share start]
[04:24] Alex Chen: Sending request now — note the partial payloads, you'll see chunked events.
[04:30] [00:05] Alex Chen: (typing) prompt: "Hi, give an answer in two sentences about the weather in SF"
[04:35] [00:10] Stream event: partial: "It's sunny in San Franci-"
[04:38] Derek Huang: Nice, that incremental display looks friendly.
[04:40] Jordan Patel: If you look at the code snippet, we use an event source listener on the client to append partials and check finish_reason. Example iOS: onChunk { append(text) if finish { commit(display) } }
[04:57] Sara Lopez: How do we handle duplicate token charges if the client reconnects and server replays previous tokens?
[05:02] Alex Chen: We attach request_id and idempotency_key; server-side we detect duplicate ids within a 30s window and dedupe. For longer-lived sessions we recommend storing a session digest and using it as idempotency key.
[05:18] Maya Ortiz: Can you explain more about quantization recommendations? We heard quantized models are cheaper but lower quality.
[05:24] Jordan Patel: We suggest int8 quant for latency-sensitive, low-cost paths. For assistant-style tasks where quality matters, use fp16 or bfloat16 if available. Our Optimize tool will recommend quant levels per workload and show expected quality delta.
[05:42] Derek Huang: Are there built-in SDK timeouts for streams? We need to avoid hung listeners.
[05:47] Jordan Patel: Yes, SDKs have sensible defaults: stream idle timeout (60s), overall request timeout (120s), and heartbeat pings. You can override.
[05:57] Alex Chen: Quick architecture note — for mobile we usually do light context on-device and keep long-term context server-side to reduce token costs. You can also do client-side compression of history (e.g., extractive summaries) before sending.
[06:13] Sara Lopez: Any red flags for implementing in our React Native app?
[06:17] Derek Huang: We're using sockets for other realtime features, might use EventSource polyfill.
[06:21] Jordan Patel: Works fine. We have RN examples. Just be careful with memory on older devices when buffering large token streams.
[06:31] Maya Ortiz: Let's talk about concurrency — can we set per-customer concurrency limits to control spend?
[06:35] Alex Chen: Yes, per-key rate limits and per-route quotas are supported. You can set burst windows and throttle; console will show when you're hitting limits.
[06:44] Sara Lopez: We also need to support offline fallbacks — if network down, we want graceful error UI not infinite spinner.
[06:50] Jordan Patel: Recommended pattern: show last known partial content, display 'connection lost' state, then attempt background retry with backoff. If failed, show a cached fallback response.
[07:02] Derek Huang: For POC, we'll want to measure tokens per session and latency distributions across 3 regions.
[07:07] Alex Chen: Perfect, send sample session logs and region preference and we'll run a 72-hour benchmark and deliver a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and cost-per-session.
[07:19] Maya Ortiz: On monitoring, can we alert on quality regressions? E.g., sudden increase in nonsensical completions after a model bump.
[07:25] Jordan Patel: Yes, Optimize ties prompt/eval sets to production traffic and triggers regression alerts if metrics cross thresholds. You can roll back model version with a canary or automatic fallback policy.
[07:39] Sara Lopez: If we start with hosted and later want to move to Private, how painless is migration?
[07:44] Alex Chen: We designed the API and configs to be identical across modes; you'd swap endpoint and credentials and can pin model versions. Some private-only features like custom KMS need additional setup but code changes are minimal.
[07:58] [screen share stop]
[08:00] Derek Huang: A few nitty-gritty items — does the hosted API support multipart responses for images (we might add image gen later)?
[08:07] Jordan Patel: Yes, image assets are supported by the generations endpoint and can be streamed as base64 chunks or referenced URLs. We'll send the image streaming guide.
[08:16] Alex Chen: Quick demo of a retry: i'll simulate a disconnect and then reconnect with same idempotency key.
[08:21] [simulation]
[08:30] Alex Chen: You see, client reconnects and we resume by re-sending last context with idempotency key; server dedupes and returns the remainder.
[08:38] Maya Ortiz: That resume behavior is crucial for user experience.
[08:41] Sara Lopez: What about edge cases — truncated tokens mid-word causing weird UI?
[08:46] Jordan Patel: Client-side smoothing and small lookahead buffering fixes most. Also set tokenizer chunk boundaries sensibly if you're doing whole-word rendering.
[08:58] Derek Huang: Ok we're getting good. Let's cover pricing quick — what are the hosted tiers for chat?
[09:03] Alex Chen: Hosted pricing is per-token for input and output; we have a base plan with rate limits and an enterprise tier with committed spend and SLA. I'll follow up with a calc for your mobile-centric usage pattern.
[09:17] Maya Ortiz: Can you also include an example of cost for 1M messages a month with average 150 tokens each?
[09:22] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll include a spreadsheet line item for that scenario.
[09:29] Sara Lopez: Any regulatory notes for healthcare-ish content? We may eventually surface medical QAs.
[09:33] Jordan Patel: For regulated content, Private deployment within your VPC and customer-managed KMS is recommended; plus we support audit logs and higher retention. We'll loop in our compliance team if needed.
[09:46] Derek Huang: Last tech question: what about latency across APAC? We need reasonable p99s for Sydney and Tokyo.
[09:51] Alex Chen: We have regions in APAC — performance will depend on model and instance type. We'll include region-specific p50/p95/p99 in the POC results.
[10:02] Maya Ortiz: Great, what's the next step timeline?
[10:05] Alex Chen: Proposed POC kickoff week of 2027-04-19, 2-week run, deliverables: benchmark worksheet, recommended param profiles, and SDK snippets.
[10:16] Sara Lopez: Sounds good.
[10:18] Alex Chen: Ok wrap up — i'll send pricing + security docs, Jordan will share streaming-retry code and RN examples, Derek will upload logs, and we'll set the POC invite. Thanks everyone.
[10:30] Derek Huang: Thanks.
[10:32] Maya Ortiz: Thanks all.
[10:34] Sara Lopez: Thank you.
[10:36] Alex Chen: Bye.
[52:00] [call end]
